claims.text: A marketing objective is a goal set for the marketing function of a business, stating what marketing is to achieve and by when.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Marketing objectives commonly used include raising sales volume or sales value, raising market share, entering a new market or a new segment, improving brand awareness or brand image, launching a stated number of new products, and raising the proportion of customers who buy again.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A marketing objective is more usable when it states a measure, a quantity and a deadline: raising market share from 12% to 15% within two years can be checked, while selling more cannot.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Marketing objectives shape the marketing decisions that follow - which customers to aim at, what to charge, where to sell and how to promote - and they give the business a standard against which the results of those decisions are later judged.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A target expressed for the whole business, such as raising profit by 10%, is a corporate objective rather than a marketing objective. A marketing objective names something the marketing function can itself deliver, such as share, awareness, sales volume or retention.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A corporate objective is a goal for the whole business, set by its senior managers; functional objectives - marketing, operations, human resources and finance - are set to support it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Marketing objectives are normally derived from the corporate objective, so a change in what the business as a whole is trying to achieve usually changes what marketing is asked to deliver. A corporate objective of growth points marketing towards volume, share and new segments; a corporate objective of survival in a downturn points it towards holding existing customers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A marketing objective is reached through the other functions as well as marketing: extra sales need operations capacity to make the product, staff to serve it and finance to fund the stock and the credit given to customers. Where one of those is missing, the marketing objective is likely to be missed however well the marketing itself is done.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Where a marketing objective pulls against the corporate objective - chasing volume with discounts while the business is trying to build a premium position - spending on marketing may work against the position the business is paying to build, so alignment is checked before the objective is set rather than after.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Demand is the quantity of a product that customers are willing and able to buy at a given price over a period of time.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Supply is the quantity of a product that businesses are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price over a period of time.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Factors that influence the demand for a business's product include its price, the incomes of its customers, the prices of substitutes and of complementary products, tastes and fashion, the season, the size and age structure of the population it sells to, the promotion it does, expectations about future prices, and the availability and cost of credit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Factors that influence the supply of a business's product include the cost of its inputs such as materials, labour and energy, the productivity of its methods and technology, the number of businesses offering the same product, weather and harvest where the product is agricultural, taxes and subsidies, and the price the product can be sold for.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because demand means willingness together with ability to pay, a change in customers' incomes can change the quantity they buy even when the price of the product has not moved. A business selling to salaried households may therefore see demand fall in a downturn without having changed anything it controls.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An input cost that rises makes a given output less profitable at the existing price, so businesses tend to offer less of the product for sale at that price unless they can raise the price or cut the cost back. Whether output actually falls depends on how much of the cost rise the business can pass on and on how quickly it can change what it makes.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The equilibrium price is the price at which the quantity customers want to buy equals the quantity businesses want to sell, so there is no pressure on the price to move.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Where the quantity demanded at the current price is greater than the quantity supplied, stocks run down and some customers go unserved, which puts upward pressure on the price; where the quantity supplied is greater, stock builds and sellers tend to discount, which puts downward pressure on it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A rise in demand while supply is unchanged tends to raise both the price and the quantity traded. A fall in supply while demand is unchanged tends to raise the price and reduce the quantity traded. The two cases look alike in the price and differ in the quantity, which is how a business can tell them apart.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Price works as a signal in both directions: a higher price tends to reduce the quantity customers buy and to encourage businesses to offer more, and a lower price tends to do the reverse. How strongly each side responds varies between products and is one reason the same price change has different effects in different markets.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: For a business the practical value of reading demand and supply is planning. A period in which demand is expected to run ahead of what the business can supply is one in which it may raise the price, take deposits or add capacity; a period of the opposite kind carries the risk of discounting and unsold stock, so orders and production are cut back in advance.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A consumer market is one in which the buyers are households purchasing for their own use. An industrial market is one in which the buyers are businesses purchasing to use the product in what they themselves produce, or to resell it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Industrial markets tend to have fewer and larger buyers than consumer markets, purchases written to a technical specification, prices settled by negotiation rather than displayed, and decisions taken by several people over a longer period.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Derived demand is demand for a product that arises from demand for something else: a supplier of tyres to a vehicle assembler sells only as many tyres as the assembler's own sales of vehicles require.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Local, national and international markets differ in the number of customers within reach, the distance and cost of getting the product to them, the number of sets of rules the business has to satisfy, and whether the money it is paid in is its own currency.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Selling internationally widens the number of possible customers, which may raise sales and reduce dependence on one country's economy. It also adds transport cost and time, customs procedures, the risk that an exchange-rate movement changes the value of a sale already made, and the cost of meeting another country's rules and adapting the product to local tastes.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Product orientation is an approach in which a business starts from the product it can make, concentrating on its quality and technical performance, and then looks for customers to buy it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Customer orientation, also called market orientation, is an approach in which a business starts from what its research shows customers want, and designs the product, the price and the promotion to fit what it finds.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The practical difference is the order of the two questions. A product-oriented business asks what it can make well and then who will buy it; a customer-oriented business asks what customers want and then whether it can make it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Starting from customer research tends to reduce the risk of launching a product nobody wants, because the need is checked before the money is spent. It does not remove the risk: research can be poorly designed, answers given to a researcher may differ from what people later pay for, and a market can move between the research and the launch.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Product orientation is not simply an error. Where a business holds a genuine technical lead, or where customers cannot describe a product they have never seen, starting from what the business can build may open a market that research would not have found. The risk is that development money is committed before any customer need is confirmed.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Market share (%) = (sales of the business / total sales in the market) x 100, with both figures taken over the same period and measured on the same basis.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Market growth (%) = ((market size this period - market size in the previous period) / market size in the previous period) x 100.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Market size, market share and market growth can each be measured by value in N$ or by volume in units, and the two bases can give different answers. A business selling fewer units at a higher price may hold a larger share by value than by volume, so the basis is stated with the figure.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A market share figure depends on how the market has been defined and on the reliability of the total-market figure, which is usually an outside estimate rather than a measured total. Widening or narrowing the definition of the market changes the share without anything changing in the business.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A rising market share means the business is winning sales faster than the market as a whole is growing. That may strengthen its bargaining position with suppliers and retailers, because it is buying more and offering them more turnover, and larger production runs may lower the cost of making each unit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Market share and sales can move in opposite directions. A business whose sales fall by 5% in a market that falls by 15% gains share while selling less, so a share figure is read alongside the sales figure rather than instead of it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Growth in the market lets a business raise its sales without taking customers from rivals, which usually costs less than winning them in a static market. Growth also attracts new entrants, so a business can be selling more each year while its share of the market falls.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A falling share in a market that is growing quickly may still leave sales rising, and points to a competitiveness problem that the sales figure hides. A falling share in a static or shrinking market usually means falling sales as well, and is the more urgent of the two.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Products are classified first by who buys them and why. Consumer products are bought by households for their own use; industrial products, also called producer products, are bought by businesses to use in production or to resell.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Consumer products are grouped further by how customers go about buying them. A convenience product is bought often, cheaply and with little thought. A shopping product is compared on price and quality across several sellers before it is bought. A speciality product is one for which buyers seek out a particular brand and are prepared to travel or pay more.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Products are also classified as goods or services, and as durable or non-durable. A durable product is used repeatedly over a long period, while a non-durable product is used up quickly.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The class a product falls into shapes how it is sold. A convenience product needs to be available wherever the customer happens to be, so it is placed in as many outlets as possible; a speciality product can be sold through a few outlets, because buyers who want that brand are prepared to go to it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: In business-to-consumer marketing the buyers are many and each purchase is small, so losing one customer matters little. In business-to-business marketing the buyers are fewer and each order is larger, so the loss of a single customer can remove a material part of the year's revenue and the seller invests more in keeping each one.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Business buying tends to be formal and technical: a written specification, quotations or a tender, a negotiated price, agreed credit terms, and several people involved in the decision. Consumer buying is usually quicker, decided by one person or a household, and more open to influence by brand, packaging and impulse.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Promotion differs with the number of buyers. A consumer product is promoted through media that reach many people at once, such as radio, outdoor advertising and social media. An industrial product is promoted through personal selling, trade fairs, trade publications and technical demonstrations aimed at named buyers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Industrial products more often move directly from producer to customer, because the orders are large and the product may need installation or technical support. Consumer products more often pass through wholesalers and retailers, because the seller cannot deal with every household individually.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A mass market is a large market for a product with wide appeal, which a business serves with a standardised product aimed at most of the customers in it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A niche market is a small part of a larger market, made up of customers whose particular needs the wider market does not serve well.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Features usually found in mass marketing are large sales volumes, a standardised product with little variation, wide distribution, promotion through media that reach large audiences, several competitors selling something similar, and competition that turns largely on price.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Features usually found in niche marketing are small sales volumes, a specialised product, promotion aimed at an identified group rather than the public, a price that reflects the specialism, few direct competitors at first, and close contact between the business and its customers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Mass and niche are descriptions of the market a business aims at, not of the product category. Bottled water sold nationally at a low price is mass marketing; bottled water sourced from one spring and sold to buyers who want that source is niche marketing, in the same product category.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The advantages of mass marketing are the size of the revenue available, the lower cost of making each unit when output is large and the product is standardised, and the recognition that comes from wide distribution and heavy promotion, which makes it harder for a new entrant to be noticed.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The disadvantages of mass marketing are the capital needed for capacity and promotion before the revenue arrives, competition from other large sellers which tends to hold prices and margins down, and the difficulty of changing direction quickly once the business is built around one standardised product.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The advantages of niche marketing are that a small business with limited capital can serve a niche, that there may be few direct competitors at first, and that customers who value the specialism may accept a higher price, which can give a wider margin on each unit sold.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The disadvantages of niche marketing are that total revenue is limited by the size of the niche, that the business depends on one group of customers whose tastes may change, that a larger competitor may enter once the niche is shown to work, and that there are fewer products and customers across which to spread the risk.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Which approach suits a business depends on the capital and capacity it has, what it is better at than its rivals, and how crowded the market already is. A business without the finance to build capacity and buy national promotion is unlikely to succeed by attacking a mass market held by established sellers, whatever the size of the prize.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Market segmentation is the division of a market into groups of customers who share characteristics or needs, so that the business can aim a different offer, message or price at each group.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The syllabus names three methods of segmenting a market: geographic, by where customers are; demographic, by measurable characteristics of the people themselves; and psychographic, by how they live and what they value. A business may use more than one of the three together, for example an age group within one region.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The method is chosen for the variable that actually explains why customers in that market buy differently, and for the data the business can get hold of. A basis that divides customers neatly but does not divide their buying produces separate marketing costs without separate sales.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Geographic segmentation divides a market by where customers are: by country, region, town, urban or rural area, or climate zone.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Geographic segmentation is useful where location changes what customers need or how they can be reached - climate, the language of the advertising, distance from a shop, or whether households are connected to mains electricity. Where location does not change buying, it separates customers without separating demand.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Demographic segmentation divides a market by measurable characteristics of people: age, gender, income, occupation, family size and stage, education, religion or ethnic group.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Demographic segmentation is widely used because the characteristics are easy to measure and much of the data already exists in census and official statistics, so it is comparatively cheap. Its weakness is that two people of the same age and income may buy quite differently, so the group can be well defined and still not behave as one.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Psychographic segmentation divides a market by how customers live and think: lifestyle, values, attitudes, interests and personality.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Psychographic segmentation can explain buying that age and income do not - two households with the same income may differ because one is concerned about the environment and the other is not. The characteristics cannot be read from official statistics, so the business has to gather them itself, which makes this method the most expensive of the three to use and the hardest to keep current.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Aiming a product and its message at a defined group raises the proportion of the audience with a reason to buy, so less of the promotional spending reaches people who were never going to buy. The saving depends on the business knowing which group it is reaching, which is why segmentation and the choice of media are decided together.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Segmentation can show a group whose needs nothing on the market meets, which is where a new or adapted product can be sold with less direct competition. It also lets a small business concentrate limited resources on the customers it can serve well rather than spreading them across a whole market.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Segmentation costs money. Finding the segments takes research; serving them takes more product variants, more packaging and more separate promotion; and making several variants instead of one means shorter production runs, which tends to raise the cost of making each unit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A segment can be too small to cover the cost of serving it separately, and segment boundaries move as incomes, ages and tastes change, so a division that fitted the market three years ago may not fit it now. A business that divides its market too finely ends up with many small runs and a marketing budget spread too thin to be noticed in any of them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Segmentation pays where three things hold together: the differences between segments are large enough to change what customers will buy or pay, each segment is big enough to cover the cost of serving it, and the business can actually reach that segment with a distinct product or message. Where any of the three is missing, the extra cost arrives and the extra sales do not.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Customer relationship management (CRM) is the way a business manages its dealings with the customers it already has - usually supported by a record of who they are and what they have bought - in order to keep them and to increase what they buy.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The aims of CRM are to retain existing customers, to increase how often and how much each of them buys, to use what is recorded about them to make offers that fit, to improve the service they receive and the handling of their complaints, and to collect feedback that guides what the business sells next.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Retention is aimed at because selling again to somebody who has already bought usually costs less in promotion than persuading a stranger to buy for the first time: the business already knows what they bought and has permission to contact them. Long-standing customers may also recommend the business to others, which brings in sales the business did not pay to promote.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Recorded purchase history lets a business make a specific offer at a sensible time - a service reminder when a machine is due, a refill offer when the last one should be running out - which is more likely to be acted on than the same message sent to everyone.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The costs of CRM are the purchase or subscription cost of the software, the work of entering and cleaning the customer data, training staff to use it, the time staff spend recording each contact instead of serving the next customer, and the cost of keeping personal data secure and within the law.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The benefits of CRM are repeat revenue from customers who stay, lower promotional spending for each sale made to them, better information for segmenting the market and timing offers, faster handling of complaints, and the chance to sell related products to somebody who has already bought.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The benefits of CRM depend on conditions that a business can check before it spends. The data has to be accurate and kept up to date, staff have to use the system rather than work around it, and customers have to be in a market where they buy repeatedly. Where purchases are one-off or many years apart, retention has much less to give and the cost is harder to recover.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Holding personal data creates an obligation as well as an opportunity: it has to be kept secure and used for the purpose customers were told about. A business that loses customer data or uses it in a way customers did not expect can lose the trust the system was bought to build, so the security and permission costs belong in the decision rather than beside it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
